claim: RalA and RalB have crucial roles downstream Ras oncoproteins in human cancers.
source: The two Ral GTPases, RalA and RalB, have crucial roles downstream Ras oncoproteins in human cancers
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general assertion about the role of Ral GTPases in cancer.

claim: RalB is involved in invasion and metastasis.
source: in particular, RalB is involved in invasion and metastasis
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a specific assertion about RalB's role.

claim: Light-controlled activation of Ral at plasma-membrane promotes the recruitment of the Wave Regulatory Complex (WRC) via its effector exocyst.
source: By a novel optogenetic approach, we found that light-controlled activation of Ral at plasma-membrane promotes the recruitment of the Wave Regulatory Complex (WRC) via its effector exocyst, with consequent induction of protrusions and invasion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in the manuscript.

claim: Light-controlled activation of Ral induces protrusions and invasion.
source: By a novel optogenetic approach, we found that light-controlled activation of Ral at plasma-membrane promotes the recruitment of the Wave Regulatory Complex (WRC) via its effector exocyst, with consequent induction of protrusions and invasion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Active Ras signals to RalB via two RalGEFs (RGL1 and RGL2) to foster invasiveness.
source: We show that active Ras signals to RalB via two RalGEFs (Guanine nucleotide Exchange Factors), RGL1 and RGL2, to foster invasiveness
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: RalB contribution to invasiveness appears to be more important than that of MAPK and PI3K pathways.
source: RalB contribution appears to be more important than that of MAPK and PI3K pathways
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data comparing pathway contributions.

claim: RalB expression at protein level increases in a manner consistent with progression toward metastasis in human breast cancers.
source: Moreover, on the clinical side, we uncovered a potential role of RalB in human breast cancers by determining that RalB expression at protein level increases in a manner consistent with progression toward metastasis.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by immunohistochemistry data from patient samples.

claim: Roughly 30% of all human tumors carry Ras genetic alterations.
source: Roughly 30% of all human tumors carry Ras genetic alterations; the Ras mutation frequency is particularly high for pancreas (91%), lung (33%) and colon (51%) cancers (cbioportal) (Gao et al., 2013; Simanshu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and database information.

claim: The Ras mutation frequency is particularly high for pancreas (91%), lung (33%) and colon (51%) cancers.
source: Roughly 30% of all human tumors carry Ras genetic alterations; the Ras mutation frequency is particularly high for pancreas (91%), lung (33%) and colon (51%) cancers (cbioportal) (Gao et al., 2013; Simanshu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and database information.

claim: No effective targeted therapies can be offered to patients with tumors carrying Ras mutations.
source: Up-to-date no effective targeted therapies can be offered to patients with tumors carrying Ras mutations.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Ras proteins are still considered undruggable.
source: Since Ras proteins are still considered undruggable (Cox et al., 2014), the focus for anti-Ras drug discovery moved downstream.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Ras activates three major downstream pathways: the MAP kinases, the PI3 kinases and the Ral GTPases.
source: Ras activates three major downstream pathways: the MAP kinases, the PI3 kinases and the Ral GTPases.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: MEK inhibitor therapy turned out to be largely ineffective for MAPK pathway inhibition.
source: For example, MAPK pathway inhibition with MEK inhibitor therapy turned out to be largely ineffective (Jänne et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The two human Ral proteins (RalA and RalB) are activated by six RalGEFs.
source: The two human Ral proteins (RalA and RalB) are activated by six RalGEFs (Guanine Nucleotide Exchange Factors) (Neel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Four RalGEFs (RalGDS, Rgl1, Rgl2, Rgl3) have a Ras-association (RA) domain and are direct effectors of Ras.
source: Among the six, four RalGEFs (RalGDS, Rgl1, Rgl2, Rgl3) have a Ras-association (RA) domain and are direct effectors of Ras.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Activated GTP-bound Ras recruits RalGEFs at the plasma-membrane triggering the activation of Ral by GDP to GTP exchange.
source: Activated GTP-bound Ras recruits these RalGEFs at the plasma-membrane triggering the activation of Ral by GDP to GTP exchange.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: RalGPS1 and RalGPS2 do not bind Ras.
source: The two remaining RALGEFs (RalGPS1 and RalGPS2) do not bind Ras
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: RalGPS1 and RalGPS2 contain a pleckstrin homology (PH) domain responsible for membrane targeting.
source: their specific activators are still unknown, but they do contain a pleckstrin homology (PH) domain (Rebhun et al., 2000), responsible for membrane targeting
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: RalGPS1 and RalGPS2 contain a proline-rich motif which binds to SH3-containing signaling proteins.
source: and a proline-rich motif which binds to SH3-containing signaling proteins (Ceriani et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: RalB has a distinct role in supporting the invasiveness of transformed cells.
source: Even though, in some cellular contexts, RalA and RalB seem to have overlapping effects, several evidences pointed out a distinct role for RalB in supporting the invasiveness of transformed cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by multiple studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: RalA antagonizes the pro-migratory function of RalB in UMUC3 human bladder cancer cell line migration.
source: In the case of migration of the UMUC3 human bladder cancer cell line (K-Ras mutated), RalA seems to even antagonize the pro-migratory function of RalB (Oxford et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: RalB is required for invasion in seven out of nine K-Ras mutated human pancreatic cancer cell lines.
source: The requirement of RalB for invasion in vitro (by Transwell Invasion assay) was shown by shRNA knock-down approach in seven out of nine K-Ras mutated human pancreatic cancer cell lines (Lim et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: RalB, but not RalA, plays a role in invadopodia formation in human pancreatic cancer cell lines.
source: Consistently, another study showed that RalB, but not RalA, plays a role in invadopodia formation in human pancreatic cancer cell lines (Neel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: RalB, but not RalA, is required for the contractility-driven invasion of lung cancer cells (A549, K-Ras mutated).
source: RalB, but not RalA, is required for the contractility-driven invasion of lung cancer cells (A549, K-Ras mutated) (Biondini et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In vivo metastasis assays in mice and hamsters supported a function of RalB pathway in the formation of tumor metastasis.
source: Moreover, in vivo metastasis assays in mice (tail vein injection) (Ward et al., 2001; Lim et al., 2006) and in hamsters (subcutaneous injection) (Rybko et al., 2011) supported a function of RalB pathway in the formation of tumor metastasis, both in Ras-mutated and Rous sarcoma virus-transformed cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: RalB, but not RalA, controls the mesenchymal migration of normal cells (NRK, HEK-HT, wild-type for Ras) by mobilizing its effector exocyst.
source: Besides the cancer context, we previously found that RalB, but not RalA, controls the mesenchymal migration of normal cells (NRK, HEK-HT, wild-type for Ras) by mobilizing its effector exocyst (Rossé et al., 2006; Parrini et al., 2011; Biondini et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature from the authors' previous work.

claim: The exocyst is an octameric protein complex involved in the tethering of secretory vesicles to the plasma membrane prior to SNARE-mediated fusion.
source: which is an octameric protein complex involved in the tethering of secretory vesicles to the plasma membrane prior to SNARE-mediated fusion (Wu and Guo, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The CRY2-CIBN interaction is reversible and rapid, with response times in the order of seconds.
source: This reaction is reversible and rapid, with response times in the order of seconds (few seconds for dimerization and ~5 min for dissociation after cessation of blue illumination), and does not require exogenous cofactors.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the optogenetic system.

claim: RalGEF-CRY2-mCherry reversibly translocated to the plasma membrane upon blue light illumination.
source: Upon blue light illumination (100 ms pulses every 15 s), RalGEF-CRY2-mCherry reversibly translocated to the plasma membrane following its binding to GFP-CIBN-CAAX (Figure 1A), as shown by TIRF microscopy (Figure 1B and Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Video 1.

claim: RalGEF-CRY2 recruitment starts in less than 15 s, reaching a threefold increase in few minutes.
source: Fluorescence quantifications inside the illuminated area showed that RalGEF-CRY2 recruitment starts in less than 15 s, as expected (Valon et al., 2015), reaching a threefold increase in few minutes (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and cited literature.

claim: Upon blue light illumination, Sec5GBD-iRFP fluorescence at plasma membrane increased 1.4 fold, indicating an efficient activation of Ral proteins.
source: Upon blue light illumination, Sec5GBD-iRFP fluorescence at plasma membrane increased 1.4 fold (Figure 1D,E and Video 2), indicating an efficient activation of Ral proteins, presumably a combination of exogenous GFP-RalB, and endogenous RalA and RalB.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D, 1E and Video 2.

claim: Light-induced RalB activation was confirmed by pull-down assay.
source: The light-induced RalB activation was confirmed by pull-down assay (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Light-induced RalB activation was confirmed by a FRET-based RalB activity biosensor.
source: and by a FRET-based RalB activity biosensor (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The optogenetic activation is selective for Ral without cross activation of Rac1 or Cdc42.
source: The activation was selective for Ral without cross activation of Rac1 or Cdc42, as shown by over-expressing GFP-Rac1 or GFP-Cdc42 together with a Rac1/Cdc42 activity reporter: the iRFP-tagged GTPase Binding Domain of Pak1 (Pak1GBD) (Valon et al., 2015), which specifically interacts with Rac1-GTP and Cdc42-GTP (Sells et al., 1997; Huang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to published literature.

claim: Upon blue light illumination, Pak1GBD-iRFP fluorescence at plasma membrane did not increase, indicating the absence of Rac1 or Cdc42 activation.
source: Upon blue light illumination, Pak1GBD-iRFP fluorescence at plasma membrane did not increase, on the contrary slightly decreased (Figure 1E), indicating the absence of Rac1 or Cdc42 activation upon recruitment of RalGEF at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Local Ral activation leads to an increase in cell edge dynamics and protrusion formation.
source: A conspicuous phenotypic consequence of local Ral activation was an increase in cell edge dynamics, leading to protrusion formation (Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Video 3.

claim: The velocity maps of OptoRal cells showed an evident stimulation of cell edge dynamics after light stimulation.
source: The velocity maps of OptoRal cells showed an evident stimulation of cell edge dynamics after light stimulation (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The stimulation of cell edge dynamics corresponded to an increase of positive velocity (protrusions) and not of negative velocities (retractions).
source: This stimulation corresponded, for the majority of the sampled space and time points, to an increase of positive velocity (i.e. protrusions) and not of negative velocities (i.e. retractions).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: No changes of cell edge dynamics were observed upon light stimulation of OptoControl cells.
source: In contrast, no changes of cell edge dynamics were observed upon light stimulation of OptoControl cells (Figure 2C and Video 4), excluding non-specific effects due to illumination or to CRY2 recruitment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Video 4.

claim: The velocity dynamics were reversible and exquisitely controllable by the illumination in OptoRal cells.
source: Moreover, the alternations of dark and light periods revealed that the velocity dynamics were reversible and exquisitely controllable by the illumination in OptoRal cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) but not in the OptoControl cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and 2B.

claim: Illumination stimulates positive edge velocities in OptoRal cells but not in OptoControl cells.
source: Illumination stimulates positive edge velocities in OptoRal cells (left) but not in OptoControl cells (centre).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Inhibition of Rac with NSC23766 did not impair stimulation by light of positive edge velocities in OptoRal cells.
source: Inhibition of Rac with NSC23766 (100 µM, treatment started 1 hr before experiment) did not impair stimulation by light of positive edge velocities in OptoRal cells (right).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Treatment with NSC23766 (100 µM, 1 hr) substantially reduced (~60%) Rac1-GTP level.
source: Treatment with NSC23766 (100 µM, 1 hr) substantially reduced (~60%) Rac1-GTP level (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Ral triggers protrusion independently of Rac1.
source: These results together support the conclusion that Ral triggers protrusion independently of Rac1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results including Rac inhibition and activity measurements.

claim: RalB-depleted cells, but not RalA depleted cells, were impaired in protrusions formation.
source: However, RalB-depleted cells, but not RalA depleted cells, were impaired in protrusions formation, proving that light-controlled stimulation of cell protrusions is essentially due to activation of endogenous RalB, rather than RalA (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D for depletion validation)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Light-controlled stimulation of cell protrusions is essentially due to activation of endogenous RalB, rather than RalA.
source: However, RalB-depleted cells, but not RalA depleted cells, were impaired in protrusions formation, proving that light-controlled stimulation of cell protrusions is essentially due to activation of endogenous RalB, rather than RalA (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D for depletion validation)
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data on RalA and RalB depletion effects.

claim: There exists an interaction between the Wave Regulatory Complex (WRC) and the exocyst complex.
source: A previous work in our lab (Biondini et al., 2016) established the existence of an interaction between the Wave Regulatory Complex (WRC), a crucial regulator of actin polymerization and protrusion formations (Alekhina et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2014), and the exocyst complex (Wu and Guo, 2015), a major direct effector of Ral
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature including the authors' previous work.

claim: The exogenous iRFP-Abi1 is correctly incorporated into the WRC complex.
source: The correct incorporation of iRFP-Abi1 into the WRC complex was verified by size exclusion chromatography: the exogenous iRFP-Abi1, as well as the endogenous Abi1, co-eluted with the Cyfip subunit in fractions of approximately 400 kDa corresponding to the size of the whole WRC complex (Gautreau et al., 2004) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B and citation to published literature.

claim: Ral activation induced an immediate increase of iRFP-Abi1 signal at the plasma membrane, both at the leading edge and at the ventral side.
source: TIRF images showed that Ral activation induced an immediate increase of iRFP-Abi1 signal at the plasma membrane, both at the leading edge and at the ventral side (Figure 3B snapshots and Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Video 5.

claim: OptoControl cells did not show any light-dependent iRFP-Abi1 recruitment.
source: In contrast, OptoControl cells did not show any light-dependent iRFP-Abi1 recruitment (Figure 3C snapshots and Video 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Video 6.

claim: iRFP-Abi1 was recruited in OptoRal cells but not in OptoControl cells upon illumination.
source: iRFP-Abi1 was recruited in OptoRal cells but not in OptoControl cells, with a robust statistical significance (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The recruitment at the ventral plasma membrane of the AbiQ56A mutant was significantly and substantially reduced with respect to wild-type Abi1 upon Ral activation.
source: The analysis of several cells showed that upon Ral activation the recruitment at the ventral plasma membrane of the AbiQ56A mutant was significantly and substantially reduced with respect to wild-type Abi1 (Figure 3E)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The WRC/exocyst association is required for efficient translocation of WRC complex.
source: The analysis of several cells showed that upon Ral activation the recruitment at the ventral plasma membrane of the AbiQ56A mutant was significantly and substantially reduced with respect to wild-type Abi1 (Figure 3E), indicating that the WRC/exocyst association is required for efficient translocation of WRC complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data on the Abi1Q56A mutant.

claim: Illumination stimulated edge velocity of OptoRal cells expressing Abi1 wild-type, but was not effective in stimulating edge velocity of OptoRal cells expressing the Abi1Q56A mutant.
source: Moreover, while illumination stimulated edge velocity of OptoRal cells expressing Abi1 wild-type, it was not effective in stimulating edge velocity of OptoRal cells expressing the Abi1Q56A mutant (Figure 3F)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Reduction of WRC recruitment correlated with a decrease in protrusion dynamics.
source: Moreover, while illumination stimulated edge velocity of OptoRal cells expressing Abi1 wild-type, it was not effective in stimulating edge velocity of OptoRal cells expressing the Abi1Q56A mutant (Figure 3F), indicating that reduction of WRC recruitment correlated with a decrease in protrusion dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data comparing wild-type and mutant Abi1.

claim: Illumination of OptoRal cells, but not of OptoControl cells, was sufficient to induce a substantial increase of invasive capabilities.
source: Illumination of OptoRal cells, but not of OptoControl cells, was sufficient to induce a substantial increase of invasive capabilities (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: OptoRal cells expressing Abi1Q56A failed to invade upon light stimulation.
source: Similar results were obtained upon expression of the wild-type Abi1 subunit of WRC complex, whereas OptoRal cells expressing Abi1Q56A (the allele specifically impaired in its binding to exocyst [Biondini et al., 2016]) failed to invade upon light stimulation (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and citation to published literature.

claim: Activation of Ral drives cell invasion by recruiting WRC via the exocyst.
source: These results strongly support the conclusion that activation of Ral drives cell invasion by recruiting WRC via the exocyst.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results on invasion assays with different Abi1 variants.

claim: HEK-HT cells develop a tumorigenic, invasive and metastatic phenotype in vivo upon expression of oncogenic H-RasV12.
source: To evaluate the contribution of Ral activation downstream oncogenic Ras in cell invasion, we took advantage of the fact that HEK-HT cells, non-transformed, develop a tumorigenic, invasive and metastatic phenotype in vivo upon expression of oncogenic H-RasV12 (Hahn et al., 1999; O'Hayer and Counter, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: HEK-HT cells did not invade at all, while HEK-HT-RasV12 displayed a strong invasive capacity in both Transwell and Inverted Invasion assays.
source: In both assays, we found as expected that HEK-HT cells did not invade at all, while HEK-HT-RasV12 displayed a strong invasive capacity (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: HEK-HT-RasV12 cells invaded as multi-cellular clusters in the 3D collagen gel.
source: Interestingly, the HEK-HT-RasV12 cells invaded as multi-cellular clusters in the 3D collagen gel (Figure 5B, photos below).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The silencing of RalB impaired Transwell invasion of HEK-HTRasV12 cells by approximately 60%.
source: In HEK-HTRasV12 cells, the silencing of RalB impaired Transwell invasion of approximatively 60%, the silencing of RalA had not effect, and the silencing of both RalB and RalA reached up to 90% invasion inhibition (Figure 5C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The silencing of RalA had no effect on Transwell invasion of HEK-HTRasV12 cells.
source: In HEK-HTRasV12 cells, the silencing of RalB impaired Transwell invasion of approximatively 60%, the silencing of RalA had not effect, and the silencing of both RalB and RalA reached up to 90% invasion inhibition (Figure 5C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The silencing of both RalB and RalA reached up to 90% invasion inhibition in HEK-HTRasV12 cells.
source: In HEK-HTRasV12 cells, the silencing of RalB impaired Transwell invasion of approximatively 60%, the silencing of RalA had not effect, and the silencing of both RalB and RalA reached up to 90% invasion inhibition (Figure 5C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Ras-dependent RalB activation substantially contributes to the invasive phenotype of Ras-mutated cells.
source: In HEK-HTRasV12 cells, the silencing of RalB impaired Transwell invasion of approximatively 60%, the silencing of RalA had not effect, and the silencing of both RalB and RalA reached up to 90% invasion inhibition (Figure 5C) (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1A for depletion efficiencies), indicating that Ras-dependent RalB activation substantially contributes to the invasive phenotype of Ras-mutated cells, and that RalA is dispensable, but it might partially compensate when RalB is absent.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data on RalB and RalA depletion effects.

claim: RalA is dispensable for invasion, but it might partially compensate when RalB is absent.
source: indicating that Ras-dependent RalB activation substantially contributes to the invasive phenotype of Ras-mutated cells, and that RalA is dispensable, but it might partially compensate when RalB is absent.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data on RalB and RalA depletion effects.

claim: The RalB requirement for in vitro invasion of HEK-HTRasV12 cells was confirmed using the Inverted Invasion assay with collagen.
source: The RalB requirement for in vitro invasion of HEK-HTRasV12 cells was confirmed using the Inverted Invasion assay with collagen (Figure 5D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The double mutant H-RasV12G37 is completely impaired in stimulating MAP kinase activity but maintains Ral activation.
source: The double mutant H-RasV12G37, which is completely impaired in stimulating MAP kinase activity but maintains Ral activation (White et al., 1995; Bettoun et al., 2016) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: H-RasV12G37 showed the same invasive capabilities as H-RasV12 by Transwell invasion assay.
source: The double mutant H-RasV12G37, which is completely impaired in stimulating MAP kinase activity but maintains Ral activation (White et al., 1995; Bettoun et al., 2016) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), showed the same invasive capabilities by Transwell invasion assay as compared with H-RasV12 (Figure 5E, center)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Ras-dependent MAPK hyper-activation is dispensable to drive efficient invasion in HEK-HT-RasV12 cells.
source: The double mutant H-RasV12G37, which is completely impaired in stimulating MAP kinase activity but maintains Ral activation (White et al., 1995; Bettoun et al., 2016) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), showed the same invasive capabilities by Transwell invasion assay as compared with H-RasV12 (Figure 5E, center), indicating that Ras-dependent MAPK hyper-activation is dispensable to drive efficient invasion, in this genetically controlled cell model.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data comparing H-RasV12 and H-RasV12G37.

claim: PIK90-treated HEK-HT-RasV12G37 cells are still capable to invade as efficiently as untreated HEK-HT-RasV12G37 and HEK-HT-RasV12 cells.
source: PIK90-treated HEK-HT-RasV12G37 cells are still capable to invade as efficiently as untreated HEK-HT-RasV12G37 and HEK-HT-RasV12 cells (Figure 5E, right)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Ras-dependent PI3K hyper-activation is dispensable to drive efficient Transwell invasion in HEK-HT-RasV12 cells.
source: PIK90-treated HEK-HT-RasV12G37 cells are still capable to invade as efficiently as untreated HEK-HT-RasV12G37 and HEK-HT-RasV12 cells (Figure 5E, right), indicating that also Ras-dependent PI3K hyper-activation is dispensable to drive efficient Transwell invasion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data with PI3K inhibitor treatment.

claim: Trametinib-treated or PIK90-treated HEK-HT-RasV12 cells were still able to invade to the same extent as control vehicle-treated cells despite nearly complete inhibition of Erk or Akt phosphorylation.
source: Despite a nearly complete inhibition of Erk or Akt phosphorylation, trametinib-treated or PIK90-treated HEK-HT-RasV12 cells were still able to invade to the same extent as control vehicle-treated cells; only the combined MAPK and PI3K blockage displayed an inhibitory tendency, although not statistically significant (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The Ras-RalGEF-RalB signaling axis is necessary to promote invasion in Ras-transformed cells.
source: Taken together these results showed that the Ras-RalGEF-RalB signaling axis is necessary to promote invasion in Ras-transformed cells, while MAPK and PI3K pathways appear to be dispensable, at least in our experimental context.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results on pathway inhibition and invasion assays.

claim: MAPK and PI3K pathways appear to be dispensable for invasion in Ras-transformed HEK-HT-RasV12 cells.
source: Taken together these results showed that the Ras-RalGEF-RalB signaling axis is necessary to promote invasion in Ras-transformed cells, while MAPK and PI3K pathways appear to be dispensable, at least in our experimental context.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results on pathway inhibition and invasion assays.

claim: The depletion of RGL1 and RGL2 substantially reduced invasion in HEK-HT-RasV12 cells.
source: We thus silenced each of the six RalGEFs by two independent siRNA in HEK-HT-RasV12 cells. The depletion of RGL1 and RGL2 substantially reduced invasion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: RLGL3, RalGDS and RalGPS1 were clearly not required for invasion in HEK-HT-RasV12 cells.
source: RLGL3, RalGDS and RalGPS1 were clearly not required for invasion, while RalGPS2 silencing showed a potential inhibitory effect, even though statistically not significant (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: RGL1 and RGL2 are the molecular actors that promote invasion down-stream oncogenic Ras by activating RalB.
source: RGL1 and RGL2 have a Ras-association domain (RA). We therefore concluded that RGL1 and RGL2 are the molecular actors that promote invasion down-stream oncogenic Ras by activating RalB.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data on RalGEF depletion effects and knowledge about RA domains.

claim: Endogenous RGL2 localization is increased at the cell edges of HEK-HTRasV12 transformed cells as compared to HEK-HT.
source: By immunofluorescence staining, we found that endogenous RGL2 (Figure 6B) and RalB (Figure 6C) were more recruited at cell edges in HEK-HTRasV12 cells with respect to normal HEK-HT cells
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Endogenous RalB localization is increased at the cell edges of HEK-HTRasV12 transformed cells as compared to HEK-HT.
source: By immunofluorescence staining, we found that endogenous RGL2 (Figure 6B) and RalB (Figure 6C) were more recruited at cell edges in HEK-HTRasV12 cells with respect to normal HEK-HT cells
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The Ras mutation frequency in breast cancers is rather low (2.3%).
source: While Ral proteins have been involved in several cancers frequently carrying Ras mutations, such as pancreas, lung, colon, bladder, melanoma (Yan and Theodorescu, 2018), their roles have not been explored in breast cancers, in which the Ras mutation frequency is rather low (2.3%) (cbioportal) (Gao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to database information and published literature.

claim: In invasive ductal carcinoma, RalB protein expression was slightly higher in luminal A and B than in HER2+ and triple-negative (TN) tumors.
source: In invasive ductal carcinoma, RalB protein expression was slightly higher in luminal A and B than in HER2 +and triple-negative (TN) tumors (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: RalA protein expression was slightly lower in TN tumors as compared to the other subtypes.
source: while RalA protein expression was slightly lower in TN tumors as compared to the other subtypes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both RalB and RalA expression was higher in tumor cells than in normal juxtatumoral cells.
source: More interestingly, both RalB and RalA expression was higher in tumor cells than in normal juxtatumoral cells (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: RalB expression significantly increased in a manner consistent with disease progression: the median H-score was = 0.5 in normal juxtatumoral cells, =1 in tumor cells of in situ compartment, =1.5 in tumor cells of invasive compartment, and = 2 in tumor cells at lymph node metastasis.
source: Strikingly, RalB expression significantly increased in a manner consistent with disease progression: the median H-score was = 0.5 in normal juxtatumoral cells,=1 in tumor cells of in situ compartment,=1.5 in tumor cells of invasive compartment, and = 2 in tumor cells at lymph node metastasis (Figure 7A,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and 7C.

claim: RalA expression did not change in tumor cells regardless of the in situ, invasive or metastatic localization.
source: On the contrary, RalA expression did not change in tumor cells regardless of the in situ, invasive or metastatic localization (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: RalB might have a role in human breast cancer invasion and metastasis.
source: With the limitation that RalB amount does not necessarily reflect RalB activity, these results suggest that RalB might have a role in human breast cancer invasion and metastasis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data on RalB expression in breast cancer samples, with acknowledgment of limitations.

claim: RalB silencing was able to impair invasion of two triple-negative breast cancer cell lines: MDA-MB-231 (carrying the KRasG13D mutation) and BT549 (Ras wild-type).
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, RalB silencing was able to impair invasion (by Transwell invasion assay) of two triple-negative breast cancer cell lines: MDA-MB-231 (carrying the KRasG13D mutation) and BT549 (Ras wild-type) (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The mechanism by which RalB drives invasion involves the exocyst-dependent recruitment at the leading edge of the Wave Regulatory Complex (WRC).
source: By using this novel optogenetics approach, we precisely established the molecular mechanism underlying the capacity of RalB to drive invasion. This mechanism involves the exocyst-dependent recruitment at the leading edge of the Wave Regulatory Complex (WRC), a five-subunit protein complex involved in the formation of the actin cytoskeleton through interaction with the Arp2/3 complex (Alekhina et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2014)
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: RalB drives invasion independently of the small GTPase Rac1.
source: This mechanism involves the exocyst-dependent recruitment at the leading edge of the Wave Regulatory Complex (WRC), a five-subunit protein complex involved in the formation of the actin cytoskeleton through interaction with the Arp2/3 complex (Alekhina et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2014), but unexpectedly independently of the small GTPase Rac1, a well-established WRC activator and master regulator of protrusions (Ridley et al., 1992; Ridley, 2006).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data.

claim: Light-induced Ral activation was instructive in promoting cell invasion of the non-transformed HEK-HT cells.
source: We also found that RalB pathway contribution might be much more relevant than MAPK and PI3K contributions to drive Ras-dependent invasion, as ascertained by using a genetically controlled cell model: the isogenic pair HEK-HT and HEK-HT-H-RasV12 (Hahn et al., 1999; O'Hayer and Counter, 2006). Light-induced Ral activation was instructive in promoting cell invasion of the non-transformed HEK-HT cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data.

claim: Active Ras binds and recruits the two RalGEFs RGL1 and RGL2, which activate RalB.
source: Collectively our findings established the utter relevance of the activation of RalB to promote invasion. By exploiting optogenetics to study causality, we showed that not only RalB was permissive for protrusion formation and invasion, but it was instructive in absence of any oncogenic mutation. Moreover, we provide a detailed molecular model of how the Ras-RalB signaling axis governs cell invasion (Figure 6D): active Ras binds and recruits the two RalGEFs RGL1 and RGL2, which activate RalB
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the discussion and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Activated RalB binds to the exocyst complex, promoting its assembly and recruitment to the leading edge.
source: activated RalB binds to the exocyst complex, promoting its assembly (Moskalenko et al., 2003) and recruitment to the leading edge (Rossé et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature including the authors' previous work.

claim: By its direct association with the WRC complex, exocyst drives WRC to the leading edge, where WRC stimulates actin polymerization, protrusion formation, motility and invasion.
source: by its direct association with the WRC complex (Biondini et al., 2016), exocyst drives WRC to the leading edge, where WRC stimulates actin polymerization, protrusion formation, motility and invasion.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and experimental data from this study.

claim: Hyper-activations of MAP kinase and PI3 kinase pathways were not required for Ras-driven invasion in the HEK-HT and HEK-HT-H-RasV12 model.
source: Unexpectedly, using the model of isogenic cell lines HEK-HT and HEK-HT-H-RasV12, we found that hyper-activations of MAP kinase and PI3 kinase pathways were not required for Ras-driven invasion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the discussion and supported by experimental data.

claim: In a panel of pancreatic cell lines, Ral pathway was found to be more commonly activated as compared to MAPK and PI3K.
source: In support of this hypothesis, in a panel of pancreatic cell lines, Ral pathway was found to be more commonly activated as compared to MAPK and PI3K, since abnormally high Ral-GTP levels were much more frequent than abnormally high levels of phosphorylated ERK1/2 or phosphorylated AKT (Lim et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Genetic alterations in Ral genes are rare events in human cancers, occurring in only 1.5% to 2% of patient cases.
source: Even though genetic alterations in Ral genes are rare events in human cancers, occurring in only 1.5% to 2% of patient cases considering a variety of cancer types
evidence: This is stated as knowledge about cancer genetics.

claim: RGL1 and RalGPS1 are found amplified in 11% of breast cancer patients.
source: Notably, RGL1 and RalGPS1 are found amplified in 11% of breast cancer patients, meanwhile RalGAPA1, RalGAPA2 and RalGAPB are altered in 14%, 8% and 6% of lung cancer patients, respectively (cbioportal bioinformatics platform) (Gao et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to database information and published literature.

claim: RalGAPA1, RalGAPA2 and RalGAPB are altered in 14%, 8% and 6% of lung cancer patients, respectively.
source: Notably, RGL1 and RalGPS1 are found amplified in 11% of breast cancer patients, meanwhile RalGAPA1, RalGAPA2 and RalGAPB are altered in 14%, 8% and 6% of lung cancer patients, respectively (cbioportal bioinformatics platform) (Gao et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to database information and published literature.

claim: Increased overexpression and/or activation of both RalA and RalB have been observed in patient tumor samples compared with normal tissues in almost all cancer types examined.
source: In almost all cancer types examined (pancreas, colon, lung, bladder, prostate, melanoma), increased overexpression and/or activation of both RalA and RalB have been observed in patient tumor samples compared with normal tissues, regardless of their Ras mutation status (Yan and Theodorescu, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Ral-GTP level were found elevated in various tumor-derived cell lines harboring different Ras status.
source: Moreover, Ral-GTP level were found elevated in various tumor-derived cell lines harboring different Ras status, including pancreas (Lim et al., 2005), colon (Martin et al., 2011), bladder (Saito et al., 2013), liver (Ezzeldin et al., 2014), lung (Male et al., 2012) and brain (Ginn et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), RalA was found to suppress rather than promote tumor progression.
source: The only exception so far is squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), where RalA was found to suppress rather than promote tumor progression (Sowalsky et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The pharmacological inhibition of the Ras-RGL1/2-RalB-exocyst-WRC pathway holds promises as anticancer strategy.
source: In conclusion, we propose that the pharmacological inhibition of the here established Ras-RGL1/2-RalB-exocyst-WRC pathway holds promises as anticancer strategy and definitely warrants further investigations.
evidence: This is a conclusion and proposal based on the findings of the study.

claim: RalB was not only permissive for protrusion formation and invasion, but it was instructive in absence of any oncogenic mutation.
source: By exploiting optogenetics to study causality, we showed that not only RalB was permissive for protrusion formation and invasion, but it was instructive in absence of any oncogenic mutation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the discussion and supported by experimental data.

claim: The minimal GEF domain of RGL2 (1–518 aa) is catalytically active on both RalA and RalB.
source: The minimal GEF domain of RGL2 (1–518 aa), which is catalytically active on both RalA and RalB (Ferro et al., 2008), was fused to CRY2-mCherry (RalGEF-CRY2-mCherry).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: HEK-HT cells are immortalized but not transformed.
source: We stably expressed these two constructs in HEK-HT cells, which are immortalized but not transformed (Hahn et al., 1999; O'Hayer and Counter, 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: RalGEF-CRY2 recruitment reaches a threefold increase in few minutes as expected.
source: Fluorescence quantifications inside the illuminated area showed that RalGEF-CRY2 recruitment starts in less than 15 s, as expected (Valon et al., 2015), reaching a threefold increase in few minutes (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to published literature.

claim: Sec5GBD specifically interacts with both RalA and RalB in their GTP loaded forms.
source: In order to assess whether the recruitment of RalGEF-CRY2 was converted in an efficient Ral activation, we used a Ral activity reporter: the iRFP-tagged Ral GTPase Binding Domain of Sec5 (Sec5GBD), which specifically interacts with both RalA and RalB in their GTP loaded forms (Takaya et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Pak1GBD specifically interacts with Rac1-GTP and Cdc42-GTP.
source: The activation was selective for Ral without cross activation of Rac1 or Cdc42, as shown by over-expressing GFP-Rac1 or GFP-Cdc42 together with a Rac1/Cdc42 activity reporter: the iRFP-tagged GTPase Binding Domain of Pak1 (Pak1GBD) (Valon et al., 2015), which specifically interacts with Rac1-GTP and Cdc42-GTP (Sells et al., 1997; Huang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Optogenetic perturbations act in a timescale (tens of second) much faster than the ones of endogenous feedbacks (minutes).
source: Since the optogenetic perturbations act in a timescale (tens of second) much faster than the ones of endogenous feedbacks (minutes) (Valon et al., 2015), this new approach allowed us to investigate the direct consequences of Ral activation, at both phenotypic and molecular levels.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The WRC complex is a five-subunit protein complex involved in the formation of the actin cytoskeleton through interaction with the Arp2/3 complex.
source: This mechanism involves the exocyst-dependent recruitment at the leading edge of the Wave Regulatory Complex (WRC), a five-subunit protein complex involved in the formation of the actin cytoskeleton through interaction with the Arp2/3 complex (Alekhina et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Rac1 is a well-established WRC activator and master regulator of protrusions.
source: but unexpectedly independently of the small GTPase Rac1, a well-established WRC activator and master regulator of protrusions (Ridley et al., 1992; Ridley, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The WRC complex has a size of approximately 400 kDa.
source: The correct incorporation of iRFP-Abi1 into the WRC complex was verified by size exclusion chromatography: the exogenous iRFP-Abi1, as well as the endogenous Abi1, co-eluted with the Cyfip subunit in fractions of approximately 400 kDa corresponding to the size of the whole WRC complex (Gautreau et al., 2004) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to published literature.

claim: Abi1Q56A is specifically impaired in its binding to the Exo70 subunit of exocyst.
source: To demonstrate that WRC translocation is a direct consequence of its association with the exocyst, we exploited a previously characterized loss-of-interaction Abi1 mutant, Abi1Q56A, which is specifically impaired in its binding to the Exo70 subunit of exocyst (Biondini et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature from the authors' previous work.

claim: MAPK and PI3K are involved in migration and invasion of various normal and cancer cell models.
source: A huge previous literature had undoubtedly shown that MAPK and PI3K are involved in migration and invasion of various normal and cancer cell models (Keely et al., 1997; Klemke et al., 1997; Ward et al., 2001; Janda et al., 2002; Campbell et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Dysregulation of Ral might be important for oncogenesis or tumor progression.
source: Notably, RGL1 and RalGPS1 are found amplified in 11% of breast cancer patients, meanwhile RalGAPA1, RalGAPA2 and RalGAPB are altered in 14%, 8% and 6% of lung cancer patients, respectively (cbioportal bioinformatics platform) (Gao et al., 2013), consistent with the notion that dysregulation of Ral might be important for oncogenesis or tumor progression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from database information and published literature.
